newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: NTT unit seeks to avoid phone format war.
newsitem.headline: NTT unit seeks to avoid phone format war.

text.p: A unit of telecommunications giant NTT said on Wednesday it plans to work with rivals to develop next generation phone technology, in hopes of avoiding what has been shaping up as a "format war".
NTT DoCoMo, the mobile phone subsidiary of Japan national carrier Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), wants to cooperate with United States and Canadian phone carriers.
"Our hope is to achieve a single standard cellular phone technology that can be used everywhere in the world," Koji Oboshi, President of NTT DoCoMo, said in an interview.
"We are ready to work together with them (other carriers) so that their system becomes compatible with ours," he told Reuters.

Late last week, a group of American and Canadian telecommunications companies announced a plan to develop their own next-generation cellular phone technology using code division multiple access (CDMA) technology, shocking NTT DoCoMo.

DoCoMo, desperate to get into the global cellular phone market after having lost out with an analogue system used only in Japan, has been engaged in the development of its own digital CDMA technology for 10 years.
Lucent Technologies, Motorola, Northern Telecom and Qualcomm Inc said last week they would jointly develop new standards, and would not join the Japanese or European efforts.

What appeared to be a format war escalated on Monday when two leading European cellular phone makers, Ericsson and Nokia, made clear they were willing to cooperate with DoCoMo, distancing themselves from the American-Canadian group.
"DoCoMo's technology is superior," said Kurt Hellstrom, executive vice president of mobile systems at Ericsson.
He said that bringing the Japanese and Europeans together would support efforts to bring down technology costs and provide global systems.

The technology the Japanese, European and American-Canadian groups are pursuing is wide-band CDMA, a third generation cellular phone system that allows transmission of full-motion video and high quality voice communications.
DoCoMo plans to start experiments on wideband CDMA in Japan beginning next year with a budget of 60 billion yen ($539 million).

"Japan and South Korea have agreed to jointly launch the wideband CDMA service in 2001 so that the people in the two countries can see World Cup Soccer through the same cellular phone terminal," Oboshi said.
Korea Telecom and Australia's Telstra have announced support for DoCoMo's technology.
